title: Reduced local closure and strict-local component criterion
statement: Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $x,y\in X$ with $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, and let $\bar x$ be a geometric point over $x$ [def-weil-geometric-point]. Let $W=\overline{\{y\}}_{\mathrm{red}}$, $A=\mathcal O_{W,x}$ [def-weil-residue-field], and $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$; thus $Z$ is the reduced local closure of $y$ at $x$, with generic point $y$ and closed point $x$. There is a canonical identification $Z_{(\bar x)}\simeq X_{(\bar x)}\times_X W$ over $X$ [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit, def-pc-fibre-product]. It identifies the points over $y$ and their closures, including their Krull dimensions [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], with their closures in $X_{(\bar x)}$. Every point of $Z_{(\bar x)}$ over $y$ is the generic point of an irreducible component, and every irreducible component has its generic point over $y$. Consequently, some point of $X_{(\bar x)}$ over $y$ has one-dimensional closure if and only if $Z_{(\bar x)}$ has a one-dimensional irreducible component. No analogous assertion about irreducible components of the ambient $X_{(\bar x)}$ is made.

source.place: Expose XIV, Proposition 2.1.3 (reduction to the local closure and the strict-henselization component criterion)

proof.text: Choose an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $X$ containing $x$. It contains $y$, since $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$. Write $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak m\subset R$ for the primes of $y,x$. The closure of $\mathfrak p$ in $U$ is $V(\mathfrak p)$: a closed set $V(J)$ contains $\mathfrak p$ exactly when $J\subseteq\mathfrak p$. The affine clause of [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme] therefore gives $W\cap U=\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak p)$ and makes $W\to X$ a closed immersion. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization](c), $A=\mathcal O_{W,x}=(R/\mathfrak p)_{\mathfrak m/\mathfrak p}$. This is a nonzero domain: $R/\mathfrak p$ is a domain and the fractions have nonzero denominators, so a zero product has a zero numerator factor. Its zero prime maps to $y$, and every prime contains zero, so $y$ is its generic point. The unique maximal ideal maps to $x$ by [lem-weil-pbc-spec-local-ring-canonical-morphism](1). The same morphism supplies the canonical map $c:Z\to W$; its stalk map at the closed point is the identity of $A$ by clause (2).

source.place: Tags 01J3 (lemma-reduced-closed-subscheme), 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves), 01J6 (lemma-morphism-from-spec-local-ring), and 01J7 (lemma-specialize-points); ILO XIV 2.1.3, reduction to the reduced local closure

proof.text: The geometric point $\bar x$ factors through $W$, since the ideal of $W$ vanishes in $\kappa(x)$, and then through the closed point of $Z$; both factorizations use the given embedding $\kappa(x)\to\Omega$. Choose the same separable closure $K\subset\Omega$ and the same algebraic strict-henselization model $A^{\mathrm{sh}}$ for these two geometric points. Apply [lem-exc-affine-strict-local-ring-comparison] to the chart $W\cap U$ of $W$ and to the whole affine chart $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Their localized base rings are $A$ and $A_{\mathfrak m_A}=A$, respectively, by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization](c); explicitly $a/s\mapsto as^{-1}$ because every $s\notin\mathfrak m_A$ is a unit. Thus both geometric strict-local rings are identified with $A^{\mathrm{sh}}$, with the same geometric residue evaluation. The algebraic model is the one of [def-sc-ring-strict-henselization]. The structural-map equation of the affine comparison makes the resulting isomorphism $Z_{(\bar x)}\simeq W_{(\bar x)}$ compatible with $c:Z\to W$ and hence with the maps to $X$. It is the canonical functorial map of [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-functoriality](3): its ring map is local (it is an isomorphism of local rings), commutes with the structural maps just checked, and induces the identity on the common residue field $K$. The uniqueness clause of (3) therefore identifies it with that functorial map.

source.place: Tag 04HX (lemma-describe-etale-local-ring), with algebra.tex Tag 04GW (lemma-strict-henselization-different) and schemes.tex Tag 01HV

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-closed-immersion-strict-localization-cartesian] to the closed immersion $W\hookrightarrow X$ and the geometric point over $x$. Together with Step 2 it gives the required canonical identification $Z_{(\bar x)}\simeq W_{(\bar x)}\simeq X_{(\bar x)}\times_X W$ over $X$. Put $T=Z_{(\bar x)}$. The affine clause of that cited statement says that the map of strict-local rings is surjective, with kernel the extended defining ideal of $W$ on $U$. Consequently $T\to X_{(\bar x)}$ is a closed immersion by [def-weil-closed-immersion], and its underlying closed subset is exactly the inverse image of $W$ (on spectra both are $V(I\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X,\bar x})$). Every ambient point over $y$ lies in that subset, and the embedding identifies the subspaces of points over $y$. For any such point $t$, its ambient closure stays in the closed subset $T$. Its closure in $T$ is the same subset with the same subspace topology. This proves the asserted identification of closures, rather than identifying $T$ with any component of the ambient strict localization.

source.place: Tag 05WS (lemma-quotient-strict-henselization); the affine closed-immersion characterization in morphisms.tex Tag 01QO

proof.text: Write $T=\operatorname{Spec}B$, where $B$ is the canonical geometric strict-local ring of the affine scheme $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$. The map $A\to B$ is flat by [lem-sbc-affine-strict-henselization-structural-flat], applied to this affine scheme and the geometric point at its closed point. Let $C$ be any irreducible component of $T$. By [lem-sc-scheme-sober] it has a generic point, corresponding to a prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$, and $C=\overline{\{\mathfrak q\}}=V(\mathfrak q)$. The prime $\mathfrak q$ is minimal: if a prime $\mathfrak r\subsetneq\mathfrak q$ existed, then the irreducible closed set $V(\mathfrak r)=\overline{\{\mathfrak r\}}$ would strictly contain $V(\mathfrak q)$, contrary to the component's maximality. Let $\mathfrak p$ be the contraction of $\mathfrak q$ to $A$. Since $A$ is a domain, $(0)\subseteq\mathfrak p$ are primes. Apply [lem-sc-flat-going-down] to obtain $\mathfrak q_0\subseteq\mathfrak q$ contracting to zero. Minimality gives $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak q$, hence $\mathfrak p=(0)$. By Step 1, the generic point of $C$ therefore lies over $y$.

source.place: Expose XIV, Proposition 2.1.3 proof, component generic points dominate the integral local closure; flatness from Stacks 07QM (lemma-dumb-properties-henselization)(1), going-down from Tag 00HS, generic points from Tag 01IS

proof.text: Conversely, let $t\in T$ lie over $y$. Choose an irreducible component $C$ containing it by [lem-sc-irreducible-components-cover], and its generic point $\eta_C$ by [lem-sc-scheme-sober]. Step 4 shows that $\eta_C$ also lies over $y$. Since $t\in\overline{\{\eta_C\}}$, the point $\eta_C$ is a generalization of $t$. Under the closed embedding of Step 3 both belong to the fibre of $X_{(\bar x)}\to X$ over $y$. This fibre is discrete by [lem-per-strict-localization-discrete-fibres], whose hypotheses are precisely the given Noetherian $X$, specialization $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, and geometric point over $x$. The fibre carries the subspace topology by [def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Generalization persists on a subspace containing both points: every relative open containing $t$ contains $\eta_C$. In a discrete space the relative open $\{t\}$ forces $\eta_C=t$. Thus $t$ is the generic point of $C$ and its closure is exactly $C$.

source.place: Expose XIV, Proposition 2.1.3 proof, final two sentences: component containing a point over the generic point, and equality using discrete fibres

proof.text: A homeomorphism preserves irreducible closed subsets, their strict inclusions and their chains, so it preserves Krull dimension by [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Apply this to the homeomorphism of closures in Step 3. If an ambient point over $y$ has one-dimensional closure, Step 5 identifies its closure in $T$ with an irreducible component of $T$; that component has dimension one. Conversely, for a one-dimensional component $C$ of $T$, Step 4 puts its generic point over $y$, and Step 3 identifies its ambient closure homeomorphically with $C$, so that closure has dimension one. Here generic points and components have exactly the meanings of [def-sc-generic-point, def-weil-irreducible-components]. All components used are components of $T=Z_{(\bar x)}$; the closed embedding supplies no assertion that they are components of $X_{(\bar x)}$.
